claim: Hunchback genes decide in minutes whether nuclei follow the anterior/posterior developmental blueprint by reading out positional information in the Bicoid morphogen.
source: hunchback genes decide in minutes whether nuclei follow the anterior/posterior developmental blueprint by reading out positional information in the Bicoid morphogen.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key feature of the developmental system being studied.

claim: Traditional arguments based on fixed-time sampling of Bicoid concentration indicate that an accurate readout is impossible within the experimental times.
source: Traditional arguments based on fixed-time sampling of Bicoid concentration indicate that an accurate readout is impossible within the experimental times.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by calculations shown in Figure 1c and 1d.

claim: On-the-fly decision schemes based on comparing likelihoods of anterior/posterior locations complete reliable cell fate decisions within short embryological timescales.
source: We found that these more efficient schemes complete reliable cell fate decisions within the short embryological timescales.
evidence: This is the main finding of the paper, supported by mathematical modeling and simulations shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The first 13 cycles of DNA replication and mitosis in Drosophila embryos occur without cytokinesis, resulting in a multinucleated syncytium containing about 6000 nuclei.
source: In Drosophila embryos, the first 13 cycles of DNA replication and mitosis occur without cytokinesis, resulting in a multinucleated syncytium containing about 6000 nuclei (O'Farrell et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as background information with a citation to O'Farrell et al., 2004.

claim: Cell fate decisions in the fly embryo are made in less than 3 minutes.
source: the successive fast decisions on the choice of differentiation blueprints, which are made in less than 3 min (Lucas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lucas et al., 2018.

claim: The map of future body structures in the early fly embryo is set by the segmentation gene hierarchy.
source: In the early fly embryo, the map of the future body structures is set by the segmentation gene hierarchy (Nüsslein-Volhard et al., 1984; Houchmandzadeh et al., 2002; Jaeger, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple sources.

claim: The definition of the positional map starts by the emergence of two (anterior and posterior) regions of distinct hunchback expression, driven by the readout of the maternal Bicoid morphogen gradient.
source: The definition of the positional map starts by the emergence of two (anterior and posterior) regions of distinct hunchback (hb) expression, which are driven by the readout of the maternal Bicoid (Bcd) morphogen gradient (Houchmandzadeh et al., 2002, Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Hunchback spatial profiles are sharp and the variance in hunchback expression of nuclei at similar positions along the AP axis is small.
source: hunchback spatial profiles are sharp and the variance in hunchback expression of nuclei at similar positions along the AP axis is small (Desponds et al., 2016; Lucas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting studies.

claim: The amount of positional information available at the transcriptional locus is close to the minimal amount necessary to achieve the required precision.
source: The amount of positional information available at the transcriptional locus is close to the minimal amount necessary to achieve the required precision (Gregor et al., 2007b; Porcher et al., 2010; Garcia et al., 2013; Petkova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple supporting studies.

claim: Part of the morphogenetic information is not accessible for reading by downstream mechanisms as information is channeled and lost through subsequent cascades of gene activity.
source: Furthermore, part of the morphogenetic information is not accessible for reading by downstream mechanisms (Tikhonov et al., 2015), as information is channeled and lost through subsequent cascades of gene activity.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tikhonov et al., 2015.

claim: By the end of nuclear cycle 14, the positional information encoded in the gap gene readouts is sufficient to correctly predict the position of each nucleus within 2% of the egg length.
source: In spite of that, by the end of nuclear cycle 14 the positional information encoded in the gap gene readouts is sufficient to correctly predict the position of each nucleus within 2% of the egg length (Petkova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Petkova et al., 2019.

claim: Mitosis resets the binding of transcription factors during the phase of synchronous divisions.
source: Adding to the time constraints, mitosis resets the binding of transcription factors (TF) during the phase of synchronous divisions (Lucas et al., 2018), suggesting that the decision about the nuclei's position is made by using information accessible within one nuclear cycle.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lucas et al., 2018.

claim: During nuclear cycles 10-13, the positional information encoded by the Bicoid gradient is read out by hunchback promoters precisely and within 3 minutes.
source: Experiments additionally show that during the nuclear cycles 10–13 the positional information encoded by the Bicoid gradient is read out by hunchback promoters precisely and within 3 min (Lucas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lucas et al., 2018.

claim: The average concentration of maternal Bicoid decreases exponentially along the AP axis by about a factor of five from the anterior to the posterior ends.
source: The average concentration L(x) of maternal Bicoid decreases exponentially along the AP axis by about a factor five from the anterior (left) to the posterior (right) ends.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The boundary region width is 2% of the egg length.
source: Between the blue lines lies the boundary region. Its width δx is 2% of the egg length.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The half-maximum Bcd concentration position in WT embryos is shifted by about 5% of the egg-length toward the anterior with respect to the mid-embryo position.
source: The half-maximum Bcd concentration position in WT embryos is shifted by about 5% of the egg-length toward the anterior with respect to the mid-embryo position (Struhl et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Struhl et al., 1992.

claim: Berg and Purcell derived the seminal tradeoff between integration time and readout accuracy for a receptor evaluating the concentration of a ligand based on its average binding occupancy.
source: Berg and Purcell derived the seminal tradeoff between integration time and readout accuracy for a receptor evaluating the concentration of a ligand (Berg and Purcell, 1977) based on its average binding occupancy.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Berg and Purcell, 1977.

claim: The Berg-Purcell strategy cannot result in a precise anterior-posterior decision for the hunchback promoter in the short time of the early nuclear cycles.
source: However, none of these approaches can result in a precise anterior-posterior (AP) decision for the hunchback promoter in the short time of the early nuclear cycles, which has led to the conclusion that there is not enough time to apply the fixed-time Berg-Purcell strategy with the desired accuracy (Gregor et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gregor et al., 2007a.

claim: The time needed to reach the standard error probability of 32% for a fixed-time decision process soars close to the boundary up to 50 minutes.
source: Decisions are easy away from the center but the time required for an accurate decision soars close to the boundary up to 50 min – much longer than the embryological times.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The hunchback promoter contains six experimentally identified Bicoid-binding sites.
source: We limit our investigation of promoter architectures to the six experimentally identified Bicoid-binding sites (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Before nuclear cycle 13, there is little time to produce sufficient concentrations of zygotic proteins for a significant feedback effect.
source: We do not consider the known Hunchback-binding sites because before nuclear cycle 13 there is little time to produce sufficient concentrations of zygotic proteins for a significant feedback effect and the measured maternal hunchback profile has not been shown to alter anterior-posterior decision-making.
evidence: This is stated as justification for excluding Hunchback-binding sites from the model.

claim: Bcd readout is the leading factor in nuclei fate determination.
source: Following the observation that Bcd readout is the leading factor in nuclei fate determination (Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2009), we also neglect the role of other maternal gradients, for example Caudal, Zelda or Capicua (Jiménez et al., 2000; Sokolowski et al., 2012; Tran et al., 2018; Lucas et al., 2018), since the readout of these morphogens can only contribute additional information and decrease the decision time.
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting studies.

claim: No active enhancers have been identified for the hunchback locus in nuclear cycles 11-13.
source: We focus on the proximal promoter since no active enhancers have been identified for the hunchback locus in nuclear cycles 11–13 (Perry et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Perry et al., 2011.

claim: Nuclei convert the graded Bicoid gradient into a sharp border of hunchback expression.
source: Nuclei convert the graded Bicoid gradient into a sharp border of hunchback expression (Figure 1a), with high and low expressions of the hunchback promoter at the left and the right of the border respectively (Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988; Struhl et al., 1992; Crauk and Dostatni, 2005; Gregor et al., 2007b; Houchmandzadeh et al., 2002; Porcher et al., 2010; Garcia et al., 2013; Lucas et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2018; Lucas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: There exist promoter architectures that reach the required precision within a few minutes and satisfy all the additional embryological constraints.
source: The main conclusion we reach using the methodology presented in the 'Methodological setup' section is that there exist promoter architectures that reach the required precision within a few minutes and satisfy all the additional embryological constraints that were discussed previously (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The fastest promoters reach a decision within the time of nuclear cycle 11 for a wide range of activation rules.
source: The fastest promoters (blue crosses in Figure 4a) reach a decision within the time of nuclear cycle 11 (green line in Figure 4a) for a wide range of activation rules.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: High Hill coefficients in the hunchback response are associated with frequent visits of the extreme expression states where available binding sites are either all empty or all occupied.
source: As shown in Tran et al., 2018, high Hill coefficients in the hunchback response are associated with frequent visits of the extreme expression states where available binding sites are either all empty (state 0), or all occupied (state 6).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tran et al., 2018.

claim: The median bound time to DNA for Bicoid molecules is approximately 0.5 seconds.
source: We find an exponential decay, an average bound time of about 7.1 s and a median around 0.5 s.
evidence: This is calculated from simulations and stated in the text, with reference to Figure 4d.

claim: Mir et al. found short (mean approximately 0.629 s and median approximately 0.436 s) bound times of Bicoid to DNA.
source: Our median-time-bound prediction is of the same order of magnitude as the observed bound times seen in recent experiments by Mir et al., 2017; Mir et al., 2018, who found short (mean ∼0.629 s and median ∼0.436 s based on exponential fits), yet quite distinguishable from background, bound times to DNA.
evidence: This is stated with citations to Mir et al., 2017 and Mir et al., 2018.

claim: Short binding times may be instrumental in achieving the tradeoff between accuracy and speed.
source: Our results show that such short binding times may actually be instrumental in achieving the tradeoff between accuracy and speed, and rationalize how longer activation events are still achieved despite the fast binding and unbinding.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: High cooperativity architectures lead to non-exponential bound times to DNA.
source: High cooperativity architectures lead to non-exponential bound times to DNA (Figure 4d) for which the typical bound time (median) is short but the tail of the distribution includes slower dynamics that can explain longer activation events (the mean is much larger than the median).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Fast decisions require a small number of Bicoid-binding sites (less than three) to be occupied for the gene to be active.
source: Generally speaking, our analysis predicts that fast decisions require a small number of Bicoid-binding sites (less than three) to be occupied for the gene to be active.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the analysis.

claim: Adding extra binding sites to the promoter increases the computing power of the enhancer-promoter system and can reduce the time to decision to about 60% of the performance of the best architectures without enhancers.
source: We find that adding extra binding sites to the promoter increases the computing power of the enhancer-promoter system and can reduce the time to decision to about 60% of the performance of the best architectures without enhancers.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the enhancer-promoter model.

claim: Promoter structures can go significantly below the time limit imposed by the duration of the early nuclear cycles.
source: The very possibility of a balance is allowed by the main conclusion demonstrated here that promoter structures can go significantly below the time limit imposed by the duration of the early nuclear cycles.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the work.

claim: Equilibrium architectures perform very well and achieve short decision times.
source: Here, we showed that equilibrium architectures perform very well and achieve short decision times, and that out of equilibrium architectures do not seem to significantly improve the performance of promoters, except for making some switches from gene states a bit faster.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Non-equilibrium effects can increase the Hill coefficient of the response without adding extra binding sites.
source: Non-equilibrium effect can, however, increase the Hill coefficient of the response without adding extra binding sites, which is useful for the downstream readout of positional information that we formulated above as decoding.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about non-equilibrium effects.

claim: Fast decision-making architectures display short DNA-bound times.
source: Our fast decision-making architectures also display short DNA-bound times.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the identified architectures.

claim: The constraint of high cooperativity means that the distribution of bound times to the DNA is non-exponential.
source: However, the constraint of high cooperativity means that the distribution of bound times to the DNA is non-exponential and the rare long binding times that occur during the bursty binding process are exploited during the read-out.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The combination of high cooperativity and high temporal variance due to bursty dynamics is a possible recipe for an accurate readout.
source: The combination of high cooperativity and high temporal variance due to bursty dynamics is a possible recipe for an accurate readout.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The equality V=D has its underlying reason in the martingale property that the conditional expectation of probabilities for two hypotheses, given all prior history, is equal to their present value.
source: Its underlying reason is the martingale property that the conditional expectation of probabilities for two hypotheses, given all prior history, is equal to their present value.
evidence: This is stated as the mathematical explanation for the V=D equality.

claim: Higher or lower diffusion rates would slide the hunchback profile towards the anterior or the posterior end of the embryo, respectively, similarly to an increase or a decrease of the number of Bicoid binding sites.
source: Our model predicts that these changes would result in modifications of hunchback activation profiles: higher or lower diffusion rates slide the hunchback profile towards the anterior or the posterior end of the embryo, respectively, similarly to an increase or a decrease of the number of Bicoid binding sites.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model.

claim: A reduced number of Bcd sites results in a strong anterior displacement of the hb expression border compared to six binding sites, regardless of the activation rule.
source: Lastly, we make a prediction for the displacement of the anterior-posterior boundary in mutants, showing that a reduced numbers of Bcd sites results in a strong anterior displacement of the hb expression border compared to six binding sites, regardless of the activation rule (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction and shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Continuous update schemes achieve the 2% EL positional resolution in less than 1 minute.
source: In the case of the hunchback promoter in the fly embryo, the continuous update schemes achieve the 2% EL positional resolution in less than 1 min, always outperforming fixed-time integration strategies for the same promoter architecture (see Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the analysis.
